children: Vinod Mahanta Mumbai: Audit committees and management teams at India's largest companies have started preparing for a major change in financial reporting under Ind AS 118, a proposed accounting standard that could alter the manner in which companies report operating profit, classify income and expenses, and communicate financial performance to investors.

The standard is likely to have implications for finance information systems, internal controls and financial performance indicators used by management. Ind AS 118 is currently awaiting notification by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. Changes to Schedule III of the Companies Act, which governs financial statement formats, are also expected.

India has proposed implementation from April 1, 2027, for annual reporting periods beginning on or after that date, while IFRS 18 takes effect on January 1, 2027. Companies have begun discussing transition plans, though their levels of preparedness vary, said Samir Shah, audit leader at Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP. "The transition to IFRS 18 is increasingly becoming a boardroom issue," he said. Ketan Dalal, who chairs the audit committees of Zensar Technologies, Torrent Power and HDFC Life said, "Its objective is to improve comparability and comprehension.

But in today's challenging business environment, the transition will put considerable pressure on companies and audit committees." The lack of final rules and reporting formats is complicating preparations, with companies reluctant to commit to systems changes before the requirements are settled. Currently, companies report expenses by nature.

The new standard permits operating expenses by nature, function or both, depending on what provides users the most useful information, aligning India's reporting rules more closely with global standards. "The biggest topic of discussion for corporates is whether the new requirements will result in a shift towards function-wise presentation" said Abhishek Rara, Partner at Price Waterhouse LLP. "For many entities that may need to adopt this presentation, the change could require significant modifications to their processes and ERP systems.," he added. Under functional reporting, expenses are classified by the activities they support, such as cost of sales, distribution, research and development, sales and marketing, and general and administrative expenses.

Employee benefits and depreciation, currently reported by nature, may need to be allocated across functions. Companies typically present a 'gross margin' subtotal under this approach. The exercise could prove complex for companies whose cost-centre structures do not support functional allocations, requiring finance teams to work with technology, human resources and business functions to establish consistent allocation principles and supporting evidence. "The hard part is making a well-supported determination of whether expenses should be presented by function, by nature or using a combination of both," said Rara. "The answer may differ across industries and business models, and corporates will need to determine which presentation provides the most relevant summary to users." he added.

Sudhir Soni, head of audit, BSR & Co LLP said that the changes could have implications for contracts and incentive structures linked to existing self defined sub-totals such as operating profit. "Depending on the arrangements, this could require amendments to contractual terms and discussions with the relevant counterparties," he said.

Auditors say that Ind AS 118 could reshape how investors and analysts assess corporate performance by standardising key profit measures. It introduces defined categories and subtotals, including operating profit and profit before financing and income taxes. Companies must reconcile these with currently reported figures, while analysts may need to adjust models if expense reporting changes from nature to function. "Defined categories, mandatory subtotals and disclosures around management-defined performance measures aim to address long-standing investor frustration: 'operating profit' and 'adjusted EBITDA' can mean different things across companies," said Vishal Divadkar, managing partner, MSKA & Associates, a BDO International member firm. The transition will also require changes beyond the accounting standard itself, particularly for listed companies and financial services businesses.

title: Ind AS 118: India Inc Gears Up for Big Changes to Financial Reporting
